rationale: The judgment changed, so a complete assessment is returned. Three things moved it. First, the ledger now carries the Research Square preprint of the 2026 hydrolysis paper and three records drawn from it: the fine print on reaction conditions (TIK-E038, complete detoxification only at the harshest setting), and two records (TIK-E040, TIK-E041) showing the proponents assert the Mysteries' psychedelic core from ‘numerous accounts’ they do not cite beyond Pindar and Cicero. Together with the new research items on auditing Kerényi's reading of the Phaedrus (TIK-R011) and on specifying lysergamide analytes rather than ergot lipids (TIK-R009), these shift the treatment of the generator claim TIK-C008: its antecedent — that a transformative experience during initiation is attested at all — is now itself a live question, and TIK-C008 is added to the load-bearing set because if the phenomenon is a modern construction the drug hypothesis loses its motive before any cup is tested. Second, the incumbent assessment carried no steelman and no per-claim treatments in the packet; both are required, and the steelman written here (secrecy makes every countervailing record an argument from silence in the one domain where silence is expected, and the hypothesis has been right the two times it was checked) is answered nowhere in the verdicts. Third, the catalog now holds fine-grained children of the chemistry claim. Three are featured because they carry the technology cost and the pharmacological gap on which the mechanism rung stands or falls: TIK-C028 (the narrow conditions), TIK-C029 (ergometrine remaining after the peptide alkaloids are gone) and TIK-C033 (the gram-per-initiate dose arithmetic). TIK-C029 is graded provisionally with low confidence because no accepted evidence record quotes its passage; it is featured with that thinness stated rather than left out. TIK-C034 and TIK-C035 stay catalogued: one is a methodological detail and the other's anchor is not in any evidence record this edition can weigh. No case verdict changed: the roll-up remains mixed because the ladder still splits at Eleusis versus Christianity; the load-bearing set gains TIK-C008; the synthesis now names TIK-E008 as the single record whose removal would most move the case. The accounts field is populated for the first time with the five serious positions the article sets side by side; the article tells the strong and weak forms of the inherited-sacrament account (TIK-C011 and TIK-C010) as one account with two versions, so the field and the telling agree. The question is kept: the founding wording still contains every account. The article grows by a new opening section that names the five accounts with what each predicts, and by the fine print, residual alkaloid, dose arithmetic, the barley-carries-ergot base-rate problem at Pontós, the unopened ergot finds, and the analyte-specification point in the closing section; a reader could not have understood from the incumbent that the 2026 result requires a specific technology, leaves an active alkaloid behind, and that a lipid assay at Eleusis would prove nothing. To pay for that, the background and Christian sections were tightened. Crux order now leads with the Eleusis residue test and the analyte specification that makes it discriminating, then the Pontós primary and re-analysis, then replication and pharmacology, then the Christian survey and the philological audits.

article:
In September 2020, a lawyer with degrees in classics published a book arguing that Western civilization's central rite began as a drug. Brian Muraresku's *The Immortality Key* spent weeks on the bestseller lists and revived a hypothesis that mainstream classics had spent forty years declining: that the kykeon — the barley drink of the Eleusinian Mysteries, the initiation Pindar and Cicero link with knowledge of death and what follows it — was a psychedelic, and that the earliest Greek-speaking Christians inherited a version of it as the original Eucharist. A “religion with no name,” running beneath the official ones, with a spiked cup as its sacrament.

The thesis sounds like one claim. It is a ladder of them, and the state of the evidence changes drastically from rung to rung. The bottom has been settled by laboratory chemistry within the last six years. The top is contradicted by the earliest documents we have. The rungs in between — the ones the book actually stands on — turn on a handful of physical tests that, remarkably, nobody has ever run.

## Five accounts of one cup

Before the evidence, the contenders. Five serious accounts are in play, and they do not sort neatly into “for” and “against.”

- **The drugged kykeon.** Ergot growing on the sanctuary's barley, processed in wood-ash lye, supplied lysergamides related to LSD; the initiates' visions were pharmacological. It predicts ergot-derived alkaloids in Eleusinian drinking vessels, and a preparation that reliably gives a profound, mostly positive experience at a dose one person could be served.
- **The ritual machine.** Days of fasting, procession, secrecy, darkness and light, ritual drama and mass emotion in a hall built for the purpose were enough on their own. The kykeon was what its recipe says. It predicts cereal and mint in the cups and nothing else — and a modern literature showing that drug-free ritual can produce experiences of the reported intensity.
- **A phenomenon that may not need explaining.** The “life-changing vision” both sides argue over may itself be a modern reading of a few ancient lines about afterlife hopes. If no ancient text attests a transformative experience *during* initiation, the drug-versus-ritual argument has nothing to explain. It predicts that a philological audit will find the beatific vision to be a twentieth-century construction.
- **The inherited sacrament.** Dionysian wine carried the pharmacology; the Gospel of John paints Jesus in Dionysian colors; the earliest Greek-speaking Christians drank a drugged Eucharist later suppressed by the Church Fathers. In its author's own scholarly register this shrinks to a weaker form — *some* early community, somewhere, spiked its cup — and this article treats the two as strong and weak versions of one account. It predicts psychoactive residues in securely identified early-Christian vessels and a traceable chain from mystery cult to church.
- **The Jewish table.** The Eucharist descends from Second-Temple meal blessings — the thanksgiving over bread and cup — exactly as the earliest texts present it, and its wine symbolism needs no drug. It predicts what the Didache and Justin Martyr describe: bread, wine with water, thanksgiving, and a hostile stance toward pagan mysteries.

In every case, what would decide between them is a measurement or an audit that has not been made. That is the strangest feature of this controversy, and the reason it belongs on this site.

## What the chemistry has settled

Start with what is no longer worth arguing about. For most of the twentieth century, claims about ancient drug use ran on iconography and inference — a mushroom-shaped carving here, a poppy goddess there — and could be dismissed accordingly. Residue chemistry ended that era. On the altars of an eighth-century BCE Judahite shrine at Tel Arad, cannabis burned with animal dung. In human hair from a Bronze Age cult cave on Menorca, measured directly in the tissue: ephedrine, atropine, scopolamine. In a Ptolemaic Egyptian mug shaped like the god Bes, a fermented multi-plant preparation including harmal and blue lotus — though the mug was bought on the Cairo art market, so its chemistry is stronger than its provenance. At a California rock-art site, chewed wads of hallucinogenic Datura tucked into ceiling cracks. [People in the ancient world really did take mind-altering substances in religious settings]{claim=TIK-C001}: that is now direct chemical fact, several times over, from independent teams on independent materials.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P01}

The first-century pharmacopeia points the same way for wine. Dioscorides, as Muraresku summarizes him, describes [wines deliberately compounded with psychoactive plants]{claim=TIK-C002} — henbane, mandrake, black nightshade, this last credited with producing “not unpleasant visions” — and Greek routinely called wine a *pharmakon*, a drug. The summary is a proponent's and the exact passages remain to be pulled, but the capability is not seriously in dispute. These were medical recipes with stated indications; nothing in them makes a drug-wine a sacrament.

So the floor of the ladder holds. The trouble — the reason this case exists — is that the floor is routinely presented as if it supported the penthouse. A cannabis altar in Iron Age Judah is excellent evidence that ancient ritual pharmacology existed. It is no evidence that ergot was in the cup at Eleusis, and less than none that a Christian in Corinth drank it. Every rung must pay its own way.

## The drink with a published recipe

Antiquity left one recipe for the kykeon. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter — the founding myth of the Mysteries — the grieving goddess refuses red wine and asks instead for [barley meal and water mixed with soft pennyroyal mint]{claim=TIK-C003}. That is the whole list. No ancient source names ergot; none describes a processing step beyond mixing; the drink reads as a rustic barley posset with an aromatic herb. The Hymn is a myth, not a liturgical manual, and the cult was secret by law, so the silence is not proof. But everything psychoactive in the modern hypothesis is an addition to this text, not a reading of it.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P02}

The hypothesis's founders knew this and built on it anyway, because of what barley implies. Ergot, the fungus *Claviceps purpurea*, grows on cereal grains, and its alkaloids are chemical cousins of LSD, which Albert Hofmann first synthesized from ergot derivatives. In 1978 Hofmann, with the mushroom pioneer R. Gordon Wasson and the classicist Carl Ruck, proposed in *The Road to Eleusis* that ergot on the barley of the Rarian plain supplied the kykeon's secret — while conceding, in Hofmann's words, “We have no way to tell what the chemistry was of the ergot of barley or wheat raised on the Rarian plain.” In 2000 Ruck and two collaborators sharpened the idea: hydrolyze the toxic alkaloids in alkali and a safer, psychoactive preparation might result. Classics mostly declined the whole line, and it hibernated in the entheogen literature until Muraresku's book brought it back with two genuinely new kinds of support.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P03}

## The two best cards in the Greek hand

The first is archaeological, and it is the case's one hard physical datum. At Mas Castellar de Pontós in Catalonia — near the ancient Greek colony of Emporion, at a site with a sanctuary linked to Demeter and Persephone — a 2002 analysis reported [fragments of ergot inside a ceremonial vessel and in the dental calculus of a young man buried there]{claim=TIK-C004}. Substance, ingestion, and cult context together, in a Greek-influenced setting. It is the closest thing the hypothesis has to a smoking gun, and its limitations are as large as they sound. It is one analysis, performed twenty-four years ago and never independently replicated, at a site a thousand kilometers from Eleusis. This case has so far read it only through the 2026 chemistry paper's citation; even the Demeter-and-Persephone attribution of the sanctuary rests on an excavation report not yet opened. Retellings have a documented habit of hardening “fragments of ergot” into “hallucinogenic alkaloids chemically detected,” which the primary wording, as quoted, does not say. And there is a quieter problem: ergot is what barley carries. A barley vessel with ergot in it is, absent more, a barley vessel. Whether the 2002 report compared the vessel and the teeth against grain from the site's own mills and storage pits — the contrast that would lift the find above background — is exactly what reading the primary chapters would settle. Other ergot finds are reported in secondary surveys, in a Bronze Age cult area in Apulia, an Iron Age grave in Poland, the gut of a Danish bog body; none has been opened by this case, and none is a Demeter sanctuary.

{plate:IMG-TIK-P04}

The second card is chemical, and it arrived in February 2026. The standing objection to the ergot hypothesis was always toxicity: raw ergot causes ergotism — gangrene, convulsions — not transcendence. A team including Ruck and members of an entheogen-research center finally ran the 2000 proposal. Across forty-eight experiments they refluxed powdered ergot in wood-ash lye, the strong alkali ancient Greeks could make, and showed that [the toxic ergopeptides can be hydrolyzed completely while measurable amounts of the psychoactive lysergamides LSA and iso-LSA appear]{claim=TIK-C005} — about half a milligram of each per gram of ergot. “Ergot would have poisoned everybody” is no longer available as an objection at the level of possibility.

Read the fine print, though, and the experiment cuts both ways. [Complete detoxification happened only at the harshest setting — the strongest lye, the lowest ergot loading, and at least two hours of controlled hot reflux]{claim=TIK-C028}; weaker or shorter treatments left poison detectable. The feasible pathway is therefore a *technology* — a specific, careful, multi-hour alkaline operation — and no ancient source attests anything of the kind at Eleusis. The authors are candid that “the focus of the study was to demonstrate the feasibility of this transformation,” not its history. Nor did the process yield clean lysergamides: [ergometrine and its epimer remained detectable after the peptide alkaloids were gone]{claim=TIK-C029}. The paper records this without comment; that ergometrine is a pharmacologically active ergot alkaloid in its own right is this case's note, not the paper's, and it belongs to a pharmacological profile no one has run. The result has also not been independently replicated, which matters more than usual because the hands were sympathetic ones — the hypothesis's co-originator among the authors, a twenty-six-year-old proposal finally validated by its proposer. Real chemistry, published in full, that a disinterested laboratory should now repeat on blinded ergot.

Then there is the gap between a molecule and a night. From their yield the authors extrapolate that [about a gram of processed ergot per initiate would reach the literature's minimum effective dose of LSA]{claim=TIK-C033} — an arithmetic step, and a minimum. “Related to LSD” carries the popular story, but LSA is substantially weaker than LSD, and the human literature on it — dominated by morning-glory-seed exposures — is a record of [hallucinations and euphoria mixed with sedation, nausea, autonomic effects, and anxiety]{claim=TIK-C006}. The 2026 authors propose that the pennyroyal in the recipe might smooth and extend the effect, and mark the idea as untested. Whether the full reconstructed preparation, at an achievable dose, reliably delivers the best night of a life rather than an unpleasant, queasy one is a question nobody has put to the extract itself.

## The empty cell

{plate:IMG-TIK-P05}

Here is the strangest fact in the whole controversy, and both sides agree on it: **no vessel from Eleusis has ever been chemically analyzed.** Not one. The 2026 paper says so while calling for exactly that analysis — the absence “is not decisive, since no systematic research has ever been conducted or since permission for such has never been granted.” Two millennia of cult, an excavated sanctuary, storerooms of curated ceramics — and the decisive measurement has never been made. Proponents read the blank as “not yet tested”; skeptics as “nothing found.” It is an untested absence, and it leaves [the headline Greek claim — deliberately prepared ergot in the Eleusinian kykeon]{claim=TIK-C007} — with real circumstantial scaffolding and an empty cell where its direct evidence should be.

The scaffolding should not be oversold, and the counter-record is specific. The canonical recipe names nothing psychoactive. The sanctuary's finances were carved on stone and publicly audited; Kevin Clinton, who has spent a career on the Eleusinian inscriptions, notes that the accounts track the sacred grain into sacrifices and dedications, “none of it for the production of ergot or drugs.” A secret ingredient gathered free from the field would not appear in accounts, so the silence is not fatal — but it is a specific, published, audited silence rather than a general one. And the methodological critics have a point this case adopts as a rule: the literature from *The Road to Eleusis* onward shows “a pattern of presenting claims, followed by mild circumstantial evidence, rhetorically solidifying the interpretation of this evidence into a ‘fact,’ on which is built each subsequent round of conjecture.” Possibility must not be promoted into fact and then load-borne.

Beneath the attribution question sits the one that gives it its point: [did the initiates' experience require a drug at all]{claim=TIK-C008}? Modern trials show that pharmacologically occasioned mystical-type experience is real — psilocybin, in a 2006 double-blind study, produced experiences volunteers rated months later among the most significant of their lives. That proves the pharmacological route exists; it does not prove Eleusis used it. The ritual account needs no supply chain, no dosing control, and no secret technology, and it ran stable for nearly two thousand years. Yet the ritual account is asserted more often than it is evidenced, and its canonical statements have not been audited here. The 2026 authors, for their part, call the Mysteries' psychedelic core “reasonably certain” on the strength of “numerous accounts of the experience” — accounts they do not quote or locate beyond Pindar and Cicero, who, as cited, link initiation with knowledge of death and the afterlife rather than describe an experience in the hall. That opens the third account: whether any ancient text, read without the lens of Carl Kerényi's twentieth-century reading of a passage in Plato's *Phaedrus*, attests a transformative experience during initiation at all. If none does, both the drug and the ritual accounts are explaining a phenomenon a modern scholar built.

## The Christian half, where the ladder thins

The book's second act needs the practice to cross into Christianity, and the crossing is argued through Dionysus. [The Gospel of John engages Dionysian imagery]{claim=TIK-C009} — water into wine at Cana, “I am the true vine” — and some serious scholars read those passages as deliberately painting Jesus in the wine god's colors; others read the same passages as Jewish messianic abundance. Either way, a literary relationship is a claim about texts. To get pharmacology across, the Dionysian wine must have been psychedelic — Muraresku himself, at Harvard, called that “a big if” — and then an actual community must have transferred the practice, not just the imagery. He names the next gap himself: “Where are the drugs?”

What the early Christian record shows is a Jewish table. The earliest descriptions of the Eucharist we possess — Paul's, the Didache's prayers, Justin Martyr's account around 155 CE — describe bread and a cup of wine (Justin: “wine mixed with water”) in thanksgiving form. The Didache gives thanks “for the holy vine of David”; Justin addresses the pagan parallels directly and runs the borrowing the other way, calling the Mithraic meal something “wicked devils have imitated.” The nearest thing to a drugged cup anywhere in the record is hostile: Irenaeus's polemic against the Gnostic Marcus, accused of a conjuring trick that turned the cup “a purple and reddish color” and of compounding love-philters — fraud and seduction, not sacramental psychedelia. On the current documentary record, [the claim that the original Eucharist was a psychedelic potion]{claim=TIK-C011} is contradicted. [The weaker claim that some early community, somewhere, spiked its cup]{claim=TIK-C010} is neither supported nor refuted, because — the pattern by now is familiar — **no securely identified early-Christian liturgical vessel has ever been chemically tested either.**

{plate:IMG-TIK-P06}

The experts the book leans on are blunt. Patrick McGovern, the Penn Museum's pioneer of biomolecular archaeology and an adviser Muraresku consulted, calls the scientific evidence connecting psychedelics to early Christianity “extremely weak to nonexistent.” Jan Bremmer, the mystery-cult specialist: “Christianity was not a mystery cult.” Bart Ehrman: not plausible. Sympathetic readers cut the same way — Jerry Brown, himself a psychedelic-Christianity author, concludes the book “fails to make a compelling case for its grand theory,” presenting speculation as fact. And Muraresku's scholarly register concedes more than his marketing: he does not defend a psychedelic Last Supper (“I don't hang my hat on that claim”), and his own site grants that “the smoking gun remains elusive.”

That transmission rung — [a psychoactive sacrament actually passing from the Greek mysteries into the Christian cup]{claim=TIK-C012} — is the weakest load-bearing element in the structure. Cultural contact is real; wine-and-immortality symbolism is shared; and none of that needs transmission to explain, because wine and immortality are among the commonest religious symbols of the ancient Mediterranean. Beneath it sits a framework — [the Eucharist as an outgrowth of pagan mystery ritual rather than Jewish meal practice]{claim=TIK-C013} — that the relevant specialist fields reject. If the framework is wrong, any future psychedelic Christian cup would have to establish its own transmission vector rather than inherit one.

## The money, and a disclosure

The hypothesis now has institutional machinery. The Yale Ancient Pharmacology Program, supported by the Athanatos Foundation Muraresku founded, is building the residue-analysis capacity this case's decisive tests require; the funder's page says the project “reframes our understanding of early Christian ritual and its pharmacological roots,” language that appears there and not in the program's scientific papers. Its published funding statement names its supporters: E. Jhong, the Robert and MeiLi Hefner Foundation, the Athanatos Foundation, and B. Muraresku.

E. Jhong is this project's founder. Readers should weigh that: the program best positioned to test the Eleusinian and early-Christian claims is funded by the hypothesis's author, his foundation, and the founder of the site you are reading. Funding is provenance, not refutation — chemistry stands or falls on replication, not on who paid for the instrument — but independence accounting is half of this case's method, and it must include ourselves. Any future YAPP result entering this ledger carries that flag. The same discipline runs in reverse: critics' motives are context, never evidence about what was in an ancient cup.

## Where this case stands, and what would move it

Rung by rung: ancient ritual pharmacology, established. Feasible ergot chemistry, demonstrated once, under demanding conditions, by interested hands, awaiting replication. Ergot at Eleusis, weakly supported — one unreplicated Iberian analogue not yet read at its source, a workable mechanism, an empty cell at the sanctuary. The drug-versus-ritual question, unresolved, with the phenomenon itself now under audit. A psychedelic original Eucharist, contradicted by every early document. A spiked cup somewhere in early Christianity, untested. Transmission, the grand thesis, running on symbolism and possibility.

What would change our mind is concrete, and cheap. The vessels exist and the methods are routine — the same panels that found cannabis at Arad and alkaloids in Menorcan hair. Residue analysis of curated Eleusinian ceramics would move the case more than everything published since 1978, provided it targets the right molecules: ergot lipids are already used by residue chemists as a marker that *cereal* was in a pot, so a lipid assay would report “barley was here” in any kykeon vessel and prove nothing; the discriminating targets are LSA, iso-LSA and lysergic acid above soil background, with the lipid test as a cereal control. A lysergamide hit in a series of Eleusinian cups would make the drugged kykeon the best-evidenced claim of its kind anywhere; a cereal-positive, lysergamide-negative series would be the first genuine null at the sanctuary. Reading the 2002 Pontós chapters, and re-analyzing the samples, would decide whether the case's one physical datum is diagnostic or background. A disinterested laboratory repeating the lye chemistry on blinded ergot, and a pharmacological profile of the whole extract, would close or reopen the mechanism. A preregistered survey of early-Christian vessels — preregistered because the likeliest laboratory is an interested one — would convert the Christian half from analogy to measurement, in either direction. And a philological audit of the testimonia would tell us whether there was ever a vision to explain. The full agenda, ranked by what each test would settle, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The ladder does not fail uniformly, so the roll-up stays mixed rather than collapsing to one grade. The observation rung is solid: ritual psychoactive use is established by independent residue chemistry (TIK-E001, TIK-E002, TIK-E003, TIK-E004), compounded drug-wines are attested (TIK-E005), and the Hymn's recipe is what it says (TIK-E006). None of that discriminates between the accounts. The mechanism rung moved once, with the 48-run hydrolysis experiment (TIK-E008), and the preprint fine print (TIK-E038) now fixes how narrowly: complete detoxification only at pH 12.5, 5% w/v, 120 minutes, with ergometrine still present. That retires ‘ergot means ergotism’ at the level of possibility while raising the historical cost — a controlled technology no source attests — and leaves the pharmacological question (TIK-E012) open. The attribution rung splits. At Eleusis the decisive cell is empty, not negative (TIK-E009); TIK-C007 sits at weakly_supported, propped by one unreplicated Iberian find seen only through citation (TIK-E007) and pressed by the silent recipe (TIK-E015), the audited accounts (TIK-E016) and the methodological critique (TIK-E019). Beneath it, the generator claim TIK-C008 is now doubly unresolved: no record evidences ritual sufficiency, and the proponents' own premise rests on ‘numerous accounts’ they do not cite (TIK-E040, TIK-E041), so whether there is a phenomenon to explain is itself under audit. On the Christian side the record is contrary rather than empty: Justin and the Didache describe bread and wine in Jewish thanksgiving form (TIK-E022, TIK-E023), the one drugged-cup text is fraud polemic (TIK-E021), specialists reject the framework (TIK-E017, TIK-E018, TIK-E020), and the author declines the strong form (TIK-E024). The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is TIK-E008: without it TIK-C005 reverts to a 26-year-old proposal, TIK-C007 loses its only mechanism, and the Greek half slides from weakly_supported toward contradicted, pulling the case verdict with it. Independence discipline is unchanged: one performance of the chemistry by interested-network authors, one unreplicated Iberian datum, and a funding edge (TIK-E027) that includes this project's founder.
assessment.steelman: The Mysteries were secret by law, and every countervailing record in this ledger is an argument from silence in precisely the domain where silence is expected: the Hymn is a public myth, the accounts are public stone, and neither would record a secret ingredient gathered free from the Rarian field and processed in a sanctuary that never published its rite. Meanwhile the hypothesis has been right both times it was checked. The one Demeter-and-Persephone-linked sanctuary whose vessel and worshipper have been examined (Pontós) reportedly showed ergot in the cup and in a man's teeth; the one chemical test ever run on the mechanism came out positive under conditions Greek technology could supply, at a yield that reaches an active dose from a gram of fungus. The initiates' own formula — ‘I fasted, I drank the kykeon’ — places the drink at the end of a fast, the moment of maximal absorption and the moment a ritual designer would choose. The skeptical account, by contrast, has never been tested at Eleusis at all: no cup, no null, no cereal-positive-lysergamide-negative series. A hypothesis that predicts correctly whenever it is checked, against an alternative that has never been checked, deserves more than ‘weakly supported.’ This assessment does not answer that argument; it holds that two checks, one unreplicated and one unread at its source, cannot carry the weight, and that the untested cell is untested for both sides.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: In its strongest public form: the Eleusinian Mysteries administered a psychedelic kykeon whose active agent was lye-processed ergot; Dionysian ritual wine carried similar pharmacology; and the earliest Greek-speaking Christians inherited this ‘religion with no name’ as a drugged Eucharist later suppressed by the Church Fathers. The author's scholarly formulation is weaker — the Dionysian premise is ‘a big if,’ the Last Supper claim is not defended, and ‘the smoking gun remains elusive’ — so the claim exists in at least three strengths (marketing copy, popular interviews, scholarly concession). This case assesses the strong form, records the concessions as evidence, and treats ‘some community spiked its cup’ as the weak version of the inheritance account.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether ancient Mediterranean peoples used psychoactive plants ritually — post-2020 archaeochemistry settled that — nor, since 2026, over whether an ergot preparation could be detoxified with ancient technology under demanding conditions. The crux is five narrow cells: the empty record at Eleusis, where no vessel has ever been analyzed and both sides cite the absence; the canonical recipe, which names nothing psychoactive and no processing; the Pontós find, one unreplicated 2002 analysis seen only through citation, which may show no more than that barley carries ergot; the phenomenon itself, since whether any ancient text attests a transformative experience during initiation — rather than afterlife hopes read through a modern lens — is under audit; and the transmission vector into Christianity, where the earliest documents describe a Jewish table liturgy and no chain of pharmacological inheritance has been shown.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the Greek half: organic residue analysis of securely contexted, curated Eleusinian vessels, targeting LSA, iso-LSA and lysergic acid above soil background with ergot lipids run only as a cereal control — so that a predictable ‘barley was here’ is not read as a hit and a null is informative — together with reading the 2002 Pontós chapters and re-analyzing the samples, and an independent, blinded replication of the lye chemistry plus a pharmacological profile of the whole extract. For the phenomenon: a philological audit of Phaedrus 250b–c and the testimonia for any text independent of Kerényi's reading attesting an experience during initiation. For the Christian half: a preregistered residue survey of securely identified early-Christian liturgical vessels, where a documented null is nearly as informative as a hit; a positive would establish a practice somewhere, not the norm and not inheritance, which would further require an uncommon shared recipe appearing first in a mystery-cult vessel and later in a Christian one.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Eleusis produced its effect without pharmacology: fasting, procession, secrecy, darkness and light, ritual drama and collective emotion in an initiation hall — mechanisms mainstream scholarship considers sufficient and which kept the rite stable for nearly two millennia — and the ‘life-changing vision’ may in any case be a modern reading of ancient afterlife hopes rather than an attested experience. The kykeon was what its recipe says: barley meal, water, pennyroyal. Ancient drug-wines were medicine and sorcery, not mystery-cult sacraments. The Pontós ergot, if it survives re-analysis, is ergot on barley in a barley vessel unless the report shows a contrast with the site's grain, and attests at most an Iberian practice. The Eucharist descends from Second-Temple Jewish meal liturgy exactly as the Didache, Paul and Justin present it, and its wine symbolism needs no drug. This account's unpaid debt: nobody has tested the Eleusinian or early-Christian vessels that could falsify it, and its ritual-sufficiency premise is asserted more than evidenced.

components.note: The pharmacological route to mystical experience is real (psilocybin trials); ritual sufficiency is unaudited; and whether any ancient text attests a transformative experience during initiation is itself under audit.

components.label: A psychedelic original Eucharist
components.note: Didache, Paul and Justin describe bread and wine in Jewish thanksgiving form; the one drugged-cup text is fraud polemic; the author does not defend the strong form. The weak form — some community, somewhere — is untested.

components.label: Transmission from mystery cult to church (vector and framework)
components.note: Depends on three claims none of which stands; its framework rung (Eucharist from pagan mystery ritual) is contradicted by the specialist fields; shared wine-and-immortality symbolism needs no transmission to explain.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive tests are cheap, routine and untried: curated Eleusinian ceramics, the surviving Pontós samples and identifiable early-Christian vessels exist, and the methods that found cannabis at Arad and alkaloids in Menorcan hair would move this case more than everything published since 1978. The blocker at Eleusis is administrative. The one laboratory building capacity for these tests is funded by the hypothesis's author and this project's founder, which makes preregistration and independent replication urgent rather than optional.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Four independent residue studies on independent materials (TIK-E001, TIK-E002, TIK-E003, TIK-E004) show psychoactive plants in ritual settings, with TIK-E002 measuring alkaloids in human tissue. Only the Bes vessel carries a provenance caveat.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient people really did use mind-altering plants in religious settings; chemistry has confirmed it several times.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Raises the prior that a cult could have used a drug; says nothing about ergot, Attica, or a Christian meal. Every account in this case accepts it.
treatment.strongestObjection: None of the finds involves ergot, a Greek sanctuary or a Christian cup; spectacular positives with no denominator tell us nothing about how surprising any single find would be.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Retraction or failed replication of the residue studies
A blinded base-rate survey (TIK-R008) showing psychoactive additives are ubiquitous, which would lower every find's diagnosticity

claimAssessments.reasoning: The Dioscorides summary (TIK-E005) is a proponent's secondhand account in a friendly venue, but the capability it describes is consistent with the Bes vessel chemistry (TIK-E003); exact locators await the philological audit.

treatment.plainLanguage: Greek and Roman doctors compounded wines with plants like henbane and mandrake; wine was a drug delivery vehicle, not just a drink.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows the capability existed; therapeutic recipes with stated indications do not make a drug-wine a sacrament, and no account denies the capability.
treatment.strongestObjection: The record rests on the proponent summarizing a primary source not yet pulled; medical recipes are silently reclassified as cult practice in the popular telling.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Dioscorides passages, once located (TIK-R006), proving materially weaker or differently indicated than summarized
A base-rate survey showing such additives were rare outside medicine

claimAssessments.reasoning: The Hymn text is read directly (TIK-E006): meal, water, soft mint, wine refused. No ancient source in the ledger names an additive or a processing step.

treatment.plainLanguage: The only ancient recipe for the kykeon is barley, water and pennyroyal mint — nothing mind-altering is named.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Fixes the public composition the drug account must add to; favors the ritual account but cannot rule out a secret ingredient in a cult that was secret by law.
treatment.strongestObjection: A mythological aition is not a liturgical manual, and the sanctuary's actual practice could differ from the myth in either direction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A testimonium found in the sweep (TIK-R006) naming an additive or alkaline processing of the sanctuary drink
Residue chemistry at Eleusis (TIK-R001) showing anything beyond cereal and mint

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on a single 2002 analysis known to this ledger only through the 2026 paper's citation (TIK-E007); the primary chapters are unread, the sanctuary attribution rests on an unopened excavation report, and the find has never been re-analyzed. What was identified (microremains, not alkaloids) and against what site background is unknown.

treatment.plainLanguage: At an Iberian site with a Demeter-linked sanctuary, a 2002 study reported bits of ergot in a ceremonial vessel and in a buried man's tooth tartar.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only datum combining substance, ingestion and cult context, and so the drug account's best physical card — but ergot is what barley carries, so without a contrast against the site's own grain it may be background, and it is a thousand kilometers from Eleusis in any case.
treatment.strongestObjection: A barley vessel with ergot in it is, absent more, a barley vessel; the find is one unreplicated analysis whose retellings have hardened ‘fragments of ergot’ into ‘alkaloids detected.’
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the primary chapters (TIK-R010) and finding a documented site-wide contrast or alkaloid chemistry — or finding neither
Modern re-analysis of the vessel and calculus with lysergamide panels and Claviceps confirmation (TIK-R004)
Opening the other reported ergot finds (TIK-R012) to see whether ingestion-in-cult-context recurs

claimAssessments.reasoning: One weak record (TIK-E014), a proponent's summary citing named scholars, attests that the Dionysian reading is a genuine scholarly position; the same literature holds Jewish messianic-abundance readings, and the ledger carries no direct exegetical work.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some scholars think John's Gospel deliberately dresses Jesus in the imagery of Dionysus, the wine god; others read the same passages as Jewish messianic symbolism.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A literary relationship transfers imagery, not pharmacology; even if true it leaves the two further ‘ifs’ the author himself names.
treatment.strongestObjection: Water-into-wine and vine imagery are at home in Jewish messianic abundance without any Dionysian borrowing; the record is a proponent summarizing scholarship.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Direct exegetical records entered on both readings
Any evidence that Johannine communities transferred a Dionysian practice rather than a motif

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E008 (48 runs, full methods, peer-reviewed) and TIK-E038 (the preprint's stated conditions) show complete ergopeptide disappearance with LSA/iso-LSA at 0.54 and 0.48 mg/g under the optimal condition. One performance by interested-network authors, unreplicated; TIK-E010 and TIK-E011 are its lineage, not independent support.

treatment.plainLanguage: Boiling ergot in strong wood-ash lye for two hours can destroy the poisons and leave behind LSD-related compounds; the Greeks could make that lye.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Removes the classic toxicity objection at the level of possibility and is necessary for the drug account; it is not evidence that anyone did it, and it raises the account's cost by requiring an unattested technology.
treatment.strongestObjection: Done once, by the hypothesis's co-originator validating his own 26-year-old proposal, with complete detoxification only at the harshest setting and an active alkaloid left behind.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Failed or narrow-envelope replication by an unaffiliated laboratory on blinded ergot (TIK-R002)
Evidence that Greek wood-ash lye could not reach or hold the required alkalinity
Any attestation of alkaline processing at the sanctuary, which would raise the claim's historical standing

claimAssessments.reasoning: Directly stated by the source in both versions (TIK-E038, TIK-E008): complete hydrolysis only at 5% w/v, initial pH 12.5, at least 120 minutes; lower pH or shorter treatment left ergopeptides detectable. Confidence is high that the paper reports it; it remains one performance.

treatment.plainLanguage: The detoxification only worked completely at the strongest lye, the smallest amount of ergot, and at least two hours of hot boiling.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cuts against the drug account's ease: the feasible path is a controlled technology, not a happy accident of barley, and no source attests it at Eleusis.
treatment.strongestObjection: Ancient practitioners could have discovered and standardized the condition empirically, as they did other alkaline processes; a narrow window is not an impossible one.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replication showing a broader safe envelope under sloppier conditions (TIK-R002)
Archaeological or textual evidence of controlled alkaline processing in the sanctuary's economy (TIK-R006)

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim is anchored to the preprint's results but no accepted evidence record quotes the passage; TIK-E038's editorial note records ergometrine persistence as stated by the source without comment. Quantities are not in the ledger. Graded on the anchor's existence, with the thinness stated.

treatment.plainLanguage: Even after the poisonous peptide alkaloids were gone, ergometrine — another active ergot alkaloid — was still in the brew.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Bears on whether the preparation could deliver what the drug account needs: the drink is not clean LSA, and a residual active alkaloid belongs to the pharmacological profile no one has run.
treatment.strongestObjection: Without quantitation the residual may be pharmacologically negligible at the doses in question; the source itself draws no conclusion.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An evidence record quoting the preprint or published passage with quantities
A pharmacological profile of the whole extract (TIK-R003) showing the residual irrelevant — or relevant — at a gram-of-ergot dose

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E008 carries the authors' extrapolation that about 1 g of ergot per initiate could supply an active dose; the arithmetic follows from the reported yield and a literature minimum effective dose of about 0.5 mg. It is an extrapolation from one performance, and a minimum.

treatment.plainLanguage: By the paper's own arithmetic, about a gram of processed ergot per person would reach the lowest dose of LSA reported to have any effect.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Makes the drug account logistically plausible — small quantities, no visible supply chain — but a minimum effective dose is not a visionary dose, and the calculation ignores set, setting and co-products.
treatment.strongestObjection: The literature's minimum effective dose comes from a different matrix and LSA is substantially weaker than LSD; reaching the threshold of ‘some effect’ is far from reliably producing the reported phenomenology.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replication yielding materially different LSA/iso-LSA per gram (TIK-R002)
Dose modeling of the full extract (TIK-R003) showing the threshold for a profound experience is far higher

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E012 shows LSA is psychoactive but substantially weaker than LSD with prominent nausea, autonomic effects and anxiety in the human record; TIK-E013 shows the pharmacological route to mystical experience is real for a different molecule. The reconstructed extract has never been profiled; the proposed pennyroyal synergy is untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: Whether the reconstructed drink would give a profound, mostly positive vision — rather than a sedated, queasy night — is unknown; the compound it contains is weaker and messier than LSD.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides whether the drug account has a point: if the extract cannot plausibly deliver the reported phenomenology at an achievable dose, the ergot kykeon loses its motive even with the chemistry proven.
treatment.strongestObjection: Set and setting, fasting, and expectation shape the experience heavily, and morning-glory-seed data on recreational users cannot speak for a fasting initiate in a ritual designed for the purpose.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Receptor, toxicology and dose profiling of the complete reconstructed extract (TIK-R003)
A controlled co-administration test of pennyroyal constituents with LSA/iso-LSA (TIK-R013)
Independent replication changing the yield or the residual profile (TIK-R002)

claimAssessments.reasoning: TIK-E013 establishes that pharmacological mystical experience is possible, not that Eleusis required it; TIK-E019 documents the genre's habit of solidifying possibility into fact; TIK-E040 and TIK-E041 show the proponents' premise rests on ‘numerous accounts’ uncited beyond Pindar and Cicero, who link initiation with afterlife knowledge rather than describe an experience. No record evidences ritual sufficiency either, and whether any ancient text attests a transformative experience during initiation is itself under audit (TIK-R011).

treatment.plainLanguage: Did the initiates need a drug to have the experience they are said to have had — or would fasting, secrecy, drama and a crowd do it — or is the ‘experience’ itself a modern reading of a few ancient lines?
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The pivot between the drug and ritual accounts, and the door to the third: if drug-free ritual suffices, or if there is no attested vision to explain, the drug account loses its explanatory motive before any cup is tested.
treatment.strongestObjection: The ritual-sufficiency position is asserted more than evidenced and its canonical statements are unaudited here, while the Mysteries' two millennia of stable operation would be anomalous if ritual alone could not reliably deliver.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Phaedrus and testimonia audit (TIK-R011) finding — or failing to find — an ancient text independent of Kerényi attesting an experience during initiation
An adversarial review (TIK-R007) showing matched drug-free ritual does or does not produce experiences of the reported intensity
Residue chemistry at Eleusis (TIK-R001) settling the question from the other end

claimAssessments.reasoning: Positive scaffolding: a working mechanism (TIK-E008) and one unreplicated analogue seen through citation (TIK-E007). Against: the silent recipe (TIK-E015), the audited accounts (TIK-E016), the methodological critique (TIK-E019), and an empty cell at the sanctuary both sides cite (TIK-E009). The founding hypothesis (TIK-E010) is context. No measurement bears on the claim directly.

treatment.plainLanguage: The claim that the Eleusinian drink itself contained deliberately processed ergot has a plausible mechanism and one distant analogue, and no direct evidence, because no Eleusinian vessel has ever been tested.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The Greek half of the thesis; its truth or falsity decides between the drugged-kykeon and ritual-machine accounts and is the necessary first link of any inheritance story.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every countervailing record is an argument from silence in a cult that was secret by law, and the decisive cell has never been tested — the untested absence is untested for skeptics too.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Lysergamide-targeted residue analysis of curated Eleusinian vessels (TIK-R001, TIK-R009): a replicated hit or a cereal-positive, lysergamide-negative series
Re-analysis of the Pontós materials (TIK-R004) confirming or removing the analogue
Epigraphic audit (TIK-R006) of the sanctuary accounts and the kykeon testimonia

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only text in the record (TIK-E021) is hostile heresiology describing a color trick and love-philters; the field's central archaeochemist calls the evidence ‘extremely weak to nonexistent’ (TIK-E017); the program building capacity (TIK-E026, TIK-E027) has produced no result. No securely identified early-Christian vessel has been tested, so the claim is neither supported nor refuted.

treatment.plainLanguage: Whether any early Christian group, somewhere, put a mind-altering substance in its communion cup is simply untested.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The weak form of the inheritance account: a hit would establish a practice somewhere, not the norm and not descent from Eleusis; a documented broad null would largely close the Christian half.
treatment.strongestObjection: The nearest text describes stage magic and seduction, condemned as fraud, and even it does not say what the cup held; the claim currently runs on capability and analogy alone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered residue survey of securely identified early-Christian liturgical vessels (TIK-R005) with a replicated psychoactive positive or a documented null
Any independent textual witness describing an unusual ingredient in a Christian cup

claimAssessments.reasoning: The earliest descriptions of the rite — the Didache's prayers (TIK-E023) and Justin's account (TIK-E022) — describe bread and wine with water in Jewish thanksgiving form, with Justin framing the mysteries as imitation; the author himself declines the claim (TIK-E024); the strong form is fixed from his site (TIK-E025); McGovern and Brown reject it (TIK-E017, TIK-E020).

treatment.plainLanguage: The claim that the Last Supper and the earliest Christian communion were a psychedelic potion is contradicted by every early document describing the rite.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Its failure severs the strong form of the inheritance account and leaves only the weak form; its truth would have made the Jewish-table account untenable.
treatment.strongestObjection: Normative texts describe the sanctioned rite and were written to present it favorably to outsiders; a secret practice would not appear in them, and the earliest witnesses are still decades after the events.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A replicated psychoactive positive in a first-century vessel with secure liturgical attribution (TIK-R005)
A textual discovery describing the earliest rite with an ingredient beyond bread and wine

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim depends on TIK-C007, TIK-C010 and TIK-C013, none of which stands; the author concedes the Dionysian premise and the transmission step are open (TIK-E024); specialists in mystery cults, Christian origins and archaeochemistry reject it (TIK-E017, TIK-E018, TIK-E020); the strong wording is fixed from the author's site (TIK-E025). Shared symbolism is the only positive material.

treatment.plainLanguage: The grand thesis — that the earliest Greek-speaking Christians inherited a drugged sacrament from the Greek mysteries — rests on shared wine-and-immortality symbolism and on three links none of which is established.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The thesis itself; it is only as strong as its weakest supporting rung, and shared symbolism needs no transmission to explain because wine and immortality are common coin across the ancient Mediterranean.
treatment.strongestObjection: Greek-speaking Christians lived inside a world where mystery cults and drug-wines both existed, and the earliest churches' secrecy about the rite is exactly what a suppressed practice would produce.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An uncommon shared recipe appearing first in a mystery-cult vessel and later in a securely identified Christian vessel (TIK-R001, TIK-R005)
The Greek half established at Eleusis and a Christian positive both occurring
Peer-reviewed work overturning the Jewish-matrix account of the Eucharist's origins

claimAssessments.reasoning: The Didache's berakah-form prayers (TIK-E023) and Justin's account with its anti-mystery polemic (TIK-E022) present the rite as Jewish table blessing; Bremmer and Ehrman reject the mystery-cult framework (TIK-E018). The ledger holds no record arguing the framework positively.

treatment.plainLanguage: The idea that Christian communion grew out of pagan mystery ritual rather than Jewish meal blessings is rejected by the specialist fields and by the form of the earliest prayers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The framework the transmission account inherits; if it is wrong, any psychedelic Christian cup would need its own transmission vector rather than a ready-made one.
treatment.strongestObjection: Syncretism was real in the Greek-speaking Mediterranean, and normative texts written to define orthodoxy would naturally emphasize Jewish continuity and deny pagan parallels.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Peer-reviewed argument overturning the Second-Temple-meal consensus with textual or material evidence
A documented early Christian community whose rite demonstrably follows a mystery-cult form
